title: Rethinking Representation Geometry in Supervised Contrastive Learning under Long-Tailed Data

paper.title: Rethinking Representation Geometry in Supervised Contrastive Learning under Long-Tailed Data
paper.abstract:
Abstract Supervised contrastive learning and its balanced variants have demonstrated their effectiveness for representation learning under long-tailed distributions. However, although prior analyses suggest that their optimal representations may exhibit a regular simplex geometry,
whether such a geometry is indeed exhibited
remains insufficiently understood.
In this work, we present a theoretical framework for these objectives that characterizes whether a regular simplex is formed at the optimum. By applying this to representative objectives, we show that these objectives fail to form a regular simplex at the optimum because they remain dependent on the number of samples per class. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce structural balancing that can be applied to contrastive objectives, and propose a fully balanced contrastive objective that provably forms a regular simplex geometry at its optimum. Both theoretical and empirical results demonstrate that the proposed method yields a more balanced representation space and improves performance on long-tailed recognition and transfer learning tasks.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Deep learning has achieved remarkable success over the past decade, yet much of this progress relies on highly curated, balanced datasets ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ; Deng et al., 2009 ) , while real-world data often exhibit long-tailed distributions, in which a small number of head classes are represented by abundant samples while a large number of tail classes contain only a few samples ( Van Horn et al., 2018 ) . Models trained under such long-tailed distributions tend to learn skewed decision boundaries, which in turn degrades generalization performance on tail classes ( Cao et al., 2019 ; Ren et al., 2020 ) . Supervised contrastive objectives have shown promising results in learning representations from long-tailed distributions ( Kang et al., 2021 ; Wang et al., 2021 ; Cui et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2022b ; Zhu et al., 2022 ; Cui et al., 2023 ; Hou et al., 2023 ; Du et al., 2024 ; De Alvis et al., 2025 ; Yi et al., 2025 ) . As in balanced distributions ( Graf et al., 2021 ; Yi et al., 2026 ) , characterizing an optimum of a loss is important for understanding the representation geometry the loss favors. However, the representation spaces induced at the minimum of these objectives remain insufficiently understood under long-tailed distributions. Among existing methods, balanced contrastive learning (BCL) ( Zhu et al., 2022 ) showed that the loss is minimized if and only if the class centers form a regular simplex, suggesting that the ideal geometry remains optimal even under long-tailed distributions. In this paper, we establish a theoretical framework for determining whether a regular simplex is a global minimizer of a supervised contrastive objective under long-tailed distributions. We first reduce the analysis from the feature space to the class-wise center space by deriving a lower bound of the loss, whose equality condition corresponds to class collapse. We then show that a center configuration that does not minimize the lower bound cannot minimize the original loss. Finally, we derive a condition that the lower bound must satisfy for a regular simplex to be its minimizer. We apply this framework to two widely used objectives for long-tailed recognition, SCL ( Khosla et al., 2020 ) and BCL, and prove that the regular simplex is not a global minimizer of either loss. Fig. 1 shows this behavior with ImageNet samples. Angles are measured between class centers. Under (a), all three methods form a regular simplex; under (b), only FBCL forms it, whereas SCL and BCL fail. We further investigate why this result holds by examining how class imbalance affects the loss. From a balancing perspective, SCL and BCL adjust the loss only within the contrastive loss defined for each anchor, the sample for which the contrastive loss is computed. Consequently, as the losses for individual anchors are aggregated into the overall loss, the absence of balancing this aggregation leaves the loss dependent on the number of samples per class. This dependence is inherited by the lower bound, preventing the regular simplex from being a minimizer of the objective. Motivated by this observation, we present structural balancing, a method applicable to supervised contrastive objectives that balances the aggregation across anchors and removes the remaining dependence on the number of samples per class. Based on structural balancing, we propose Fully Balanced Contrastive Learning (FBCL), whose global minimizer is a regular simplex. We also analyze the effect of structural balancing on the representation space by examining how the loss penalizes the intra-class variance of each class as the loss is minimized. Under SCL and BCL, the coefficient of the intra-class variance penalty is approximately proportional to class frequency, whereas under FBCL it is approximately independent of it. This suggests more balanced contraction across classes, which is further supported by our empirical analysis of intra-class variance. We further evaluate FBCL with other contrastive objectives and apply structural balancing to other long-tailed recognition methods. Results show that FBCL and structural balancing can be effectively combined with other methods and improve their performance. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We establish a framework for determining whether a regular simplex is a global minimizer of a supervised contrastive objective under long-tailed distributions. Applying this framework to SCL and BCL, we prove that the regular simplex is a global minimizer of neither loss. • We observe that this failure occurs as a result of the remaining dependence on the number of samples per class in the loss. Based on this observation, we present structural balancing and propose Fully Balanced Contrastive Learning (FBCL), whose loss removes this dependence and admits the regular simplex as its global minimizer. • We empirically evaluate FBCL on long-tailed recognition and transfer learning, and further examine structural balancing in combination with other methods. The results show consistent improvements in classification accuracy and transferability across these settings.

sections.heading: Long-Tailed Recognition.
sections.text: Numerous approaches have been proposed to address long-tailed recognition. Re-sampling ( He and Garcia, 2009 ; Buda et al., 2018 ; Shi et al., 2023 ) and re-weighting classification losses ( Huang et al., 2016 ; Ren et al., 2018 ; Cui et al., 2019 ) were earlier methods in which the former balances the number of training samples and the latter assigns different weights to each training sample. Zhou et al. (2020) and Kang et al. (2020) propose a two-branch network and a two-stage learning framework, respectively, and show that such designs often yield better representations. Several works further demonstrate the effectiveness of these frameworks ( Wang et al., 2021 ; Zhong et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2022a ; Li et al., 2024a ) . Logit adjustment methods ( Cao et al., 2019 ; Menon et al., 2021 ; Kini et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2022a ; Wang et al., 2023 ) enlarge the margins for tail classes. Transfer learning methods ( Yin et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2024a ) enrich tail class features by leveraging abundant information from head classes. Recently, fine-tuning foundation models ( Tian et al., 2022 ; Dong et al., 2023 ; Shi et al., 2024 ) has proven effective with efficient training schemes, yet the impact of imbalanced data on fine-tuning is not fully understood.

sections.heading: Contrastive Learning under Long-Tailed Distributions.
sections.text: Contrastive learning ( He et al., 2020 ; Chen et al., 2020 ) has shown significant progress in representation learning, mostly under balanced data distributions. To address long-tailed distributions, Hybrid-SC ( Wang et al., 2021 ) incorporates the SCL loss into the feature learning branch of a two-branch network, leveraging the quality of its learned embeddings to obtain more discriminative representations. However, subsequent studies have shown that SCL itself is biased toward head classes and yields a skewed representation space ( Kang et al., 2021 ; Cui et al., 2021 ; Zhu et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2022b ) . To mitigate this issue, PaCo ( Cui et al., 2021 ) introduces parametric class-wise learnable centers, KCL ( Kang et al., 2021 ) uses the same number of positive samples for all classes, and BCL ( Zhu et al., 2022 ) balances the negative terms so that each class contributes equally to the repulsive force. TSC ( Li et al., 2022b ) assigns uniformly distributed class targets to attract the features of each class. Yi et al. (2025) demonstrates that the geometry of the representation obtained by minimizing the SCL loss is skewed under a specific scenario where all classes share the same number of samples except for one majority class. Different from previous works, we provide a framework for analyzing whether a regular simplex is a global minimizer of supervised contrastive learning objectives under long-tailed distributions, based on the form of their lower bounds. Using our framework, we study two representative objectives: the supervised contrastive loss ( Khosla et al., 2020 ) and the balanced contrastive loss ( Zhu et al., 2022 ) , both of which continue to serve as widely used bases for analysis in long-tailed recognition ( Cui et al., 2021 ; Cui et al., 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024b ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Yi et al., 2025 ; Son et al., 2025 ; De Alvis et al., 2025 ; Wan et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . We show that the regular simplex is not a global minimizer of either objective which is nontrivial for BCL, which has been shown to admit such geometry at its minimum. Building on our framework, we propose a balancing method for supervised contrastive objectives and a fully balanced contrastive loss, a simple contrastive objective whose global minimizer is provably a regular simplex under long-tailed distributions.

sections.heading: 4 Representation Geometry under long-tailed distributions
sections.text: In this section, we analyze the geometry of the global minimizers of contrastive losses. Section 4.1 develops a framework that derives lower bounds for supervised contrastive objectives and uses them to examine regular simplex optimality. By showing that non-optimality at the lower bound implies non-optimality at the original loss, we prove that a regular simplex is not optimal for either of two representative losses, SCL or BCL. Section 4.2 introduces structural balancing to overcome this failure and proposes Fully Balanced Contrastive Learning (FBCL), whose global minimizer is provably a regular simplex. Section 4.3 analyzes the effect of structural balancing on intra-class variance penalty.

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We conduct experiments on standard long-tailed datasets. We also conduct experiments on diverse downstream datasets to evaluate not only classification performance but also the transferability of representations learned under class imbalance, an aspect that has not been widely reported.

sections.heading: Long-tailed recognition
sections.text: We use ImageNet-LT ( Liu et al., 2019 ) , a long-tailed subset of ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) containing 115.8K images from 1,000 classes (cardinalities ranging from 5 to 1,280), and iNaturalist ( Van Horn et al., 2018 ) , a large-scale imbalanced dataset of 437.5K images from 8,142 classes. We report accuracy on many-shot ( > > 100 images), medium-shot (20 ∼ \sim 100), few-shot ( < < 20), and all classes.

sections.heading: Transfer learning
sections.text: To evaluate the transferability of the learned representations, we run experiments on the following datasets: CIFAR-10/100 ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ) , MIT67 ( Quattoni and Torralba, 2009 ) , DTD ( Cimpoi et al., 2014 ) , Oxford-IIIT Pets ( Parkhi et al., 2012 ) , Caltech101 ( Fei-Fei et al., 2004 ) , Flowers ( Nilsback and Zisserman, 2008 ) , CUB200 ( Wah et al., 2011 ) , Food ( Bossard et al., 2014 ) , Stanford Cars ( Krause et al., 2013 ) and FGVC Aircraft ( Maji et al., 2013 ) . We report results under both linear evaluation and fine-tuning.

sections.heading: 5.2 Dual-branch Training Framework
sections.text: We use the dual-branch framework, which is commonly used to learn better representations under long-tailed distributions ( Kang et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2021 ; Zhu et al., 2022 ; Suh and Seo, 2023 ; Du et al., 2024 ; Yi et al., 2025 ) . sections.heading: 5.4 Results
sections.text: Table 2 reports the top-1 accuracy of long-tailed recognition methods and methods combined with structural balancing on ImageNet-LT and iNaturalist. Structural balancing consistently improves over the base methods, showing its applicability and that it can be readily incorporated into other methods. Table 3 reports the transferability results, with FBCL achieving the highest average performance on both evaluations. Tables 1 and 2 show that FBCL achieves the highest results among contrastive methods based on SCL or BCL ( Wang et al., 2021 ; Cui et al., 2021 ; Cui et al., 2023 ; Kang et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2022b ; Zhu et al., 2022 ; Hou et al., 2023 ) . Results with other methods, datasets and standard deviations are provided in Appendix C.5 .

sections.heading: 5.5 Ablation Study
sections.text: To examine the individual role of each balancing method in the FBCL loss, we conduct an ablation study on ImageNet-LT. As described in Section 4.2 , FBCL contains three balancing components: positive balancing (PB), negative balancing (NB), and structural balancing (SB). Please refer to Appendix B.6 for each balancing component. From Table 4(b) , we first observe that SB reduces the disparity of intra-class variance across classes. Without SB, the intra-class variance gap between many and few classes is 0.168 for SCL and 0.195 for BCL, while adding SB reduces these gaps to 0.141 for PB+SB and 0.143 for FBCL. The results of NB+SB further show that reducing the variance gap alone is not sufficient, and that lowering the intra-class variance within each class group is also important. Comparing NB+SB with FBCL isolates the role of PB: adding PB reduces intra-class variance across all groups while improving overall accuracy. Likewise, comparing PB+SB with FBCL shows that removing NB decreases accuracy, indicating the contribution of NB. Together, these results show that PB, NB, and SB are complementary.

sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: Our theoretical analysis follows the standard setting adopted in prior geometric analyses of contrastive learning, where each batch contains all classes ( Graf et al., 2021 ; Zhu et al., 2022 ; Yi et al., 2025 ) . This setting is used to characterize the geometry of the objective at its optimum, and such analyses still provide a principled indication of the geometric tendency induced by the objective under practical mini-batch training. Within this analytical setting, our contribution is to show that the regular simplex guarantee does not hold for previous methods under long-tailed distributions, and to establish such a guarantee for FBCL. The dimensional condition is satisfied on ImageNet-LT but not on iNaturalist. The attainability of such geometric optima in large-scale training is beyond the scope of this work and remains underexplored even for contrastive objectives under large-scale balanced distributions ( Graf et al., 2021 ) ; how these geometric tendencies manifest under partial class coverage in mini-batches or when K > h + 1 K>h+1 provides an interesting direction for future study. Nevertheless, structural balancing itself is not restricted to these analytical conditions and consistently improves the methods with which it is combined in practical large-scale settings, including iNaturalist. Thus, our theory characterizes how balancing changes the objective and its optimum under the same analytical regime used in prior works, while the experiments show that the resulting mechanism remains effective under practical stochastic training.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we studied the representation geometry induced by supervised contrastive objectives under long-tailed distributions and developed a framework for analyzing regular simplex optimality. We showed that the regular simplex is not a global minimizer of SCL or BCL under class imbalance due to the remaining dependence on class cardinality in the aggregation of anchor-wise losses. To remove this dependence, we introduced structural balancing and proposed Fully Balanced Contrastive Learning (FBCL), which admits a regular simplex as a global optimum. We further showed that structural balancing makes the alignment term penalty on intra-class variance approximately independent of class frequency, and empirically observed more balanced intra-class variances across classes. Experiments on ImageNet-LT, iNaturalist, and transfer tasks demonstrate improvements in long-tailed recognition and representation transfer, as well as the effectiveness of structural balancing when combined with other methods. Our work thus provides a principled way to analyze and improve supervised contrastive learning under long-tailed distributions.

sections.heading: Appendix B Theoretical framework and proofs
sections.text: We establish our framework in three steps that can be used for any contrastive objective. Then, we apply our framework to representative objectives under a long-tailed distribution. For a given supervised contrastive objective ℒ \mathcal{L} , Lemmas 3 and 4 derive ℒ ​ ℬ \mathcal{LB} of ℒ \mathcal{L} , a lower bound whose equality condition corresponds to class-collapse (C1) . Results of Lemmas 1 and 2 correspond to consistency and characterization, respectively. Concretely, we analyze the loss through its lower bound which depends on the number of classes. To ensure that the results derived from the lower bound are consistent with those from the original loss, that is, that the geometry of the representations is consistent under both analyses, we establish Lemma 1 . Therefore, if a particular geometry configuration does not minimize the lower bound, it also does not minimize the original loss. If it does, we further derive a lower bound of ℒ ​ ℬ \mathcal{LB} whose equality condition characterizes the optimal geometry. Lemma 2 allows us to analyze a lower bound through its coefficients and characterize whether a regular simplex configuration minimizes it. With these Lemmas, our framework is as follows: Contrastive Objective ℒ \mathcal{L} Lower bound ℒ ​ ℬ \mathcal{LB} 1. B.3 Applying our framework to supervised contrastive objectives
sections.text: We now apply the framework to supervised contrastive objectives in the theorems. For each loss, the procedure is the same: 1. Derive the lower bound using Lemmas 3 and 4 . 2. From the lower bound, we identify the coefficients { a y } , { b y } , { c y } , β \{a_{y}\},\{b_{y}\},\{c_{y}\},\beta ; substitute them into the condition of Lemma 2 ; and check whether the resulting equality holds across classes. 3. Transfer the result back to the original loss by Lemma 1 . For SCL and BCL, dependence on the class cardinalities { B y } \{B_{y}\} prevents the condition of Lemma 2 from being satisfied, so the regular simplex fails to be even a stationary point of the lower bound and therefore fails to be a global minimizer. For FBCL, the condition holds since structural balancing eliminates dependence on { B y } \{B_{y}\} . We further show that this stationary point is indeed a global minimum by deriving subsequent lower bounds whose equality conditions characterize a regular simplex.

sections.heading: Optimality of SCL and BCL.
sections.text: Characterizing the optimality of SCL and BCL under long-tailed distribution is a harder problem which has to deal with numerical relationships across angles between class centers ( Yi et al., 2025 ) . Therefore, we rather investigate whether a particular geometry is attained at the minimum of an objective.

sections.heading: Balancing the aggregation across anchors.
sections.text:
Our analysis reveals that balancing within each anchor-wise loss is not sufficient to remove the dependence of the objective on class cardinality. In SCL, the positive samples are averaged within each anchor-wise loss, and BCL additionally balances the contributions of negative classes in its denominator. Moreover, Zhong et al. (2022) , De Alvis et al. (2025) , and Roh et al. (2026) have studied re-balancing supervised contrastive objectives using the effective number of samples ( Cui et al., 2019 ) or class cardinalities in the numerator or denominator; these methods still perform balancing within each anchor-wise loss . However, when these anchor-wise losses are aggregated to form the overall objective, each class contributes in proportion to its number of anchors. This remaining class-dependent weighting is consequently inherited by the class-level lower bound, which prevents the regular simplex from being optimal under long-tailed distributions. Structural balancing (SB) normalizes the aggregation of anchor-wise losses across classes. Although this operation can be viewed as a class-dependent weighting of anchor losses, its role here is determined by the geometric analysis: SB removes the remaining class-cardinality dependence from the class-level lower bound and thereby recovers the regular simplex as an optimum. FBCL combines this structural balancing with the positive and negative balancing already present in BCL. Theorem 3 states that the regular simplex is a global minimizer of the FBCL loss. sections.heading: B.4 Lower bounds of supervised contrastive objectives
sections.text: The class-level lower bounds ℒ ​ ℬ SCL \mathcal{LB}_{\mathrm{SCL}} , ℒ ​ ℬ BCL \mathcal{LB}_{\mathrm{BCL}} , and ℒ ​ ℬ FBCL \mathcal{LB}_{\mathrm{FBCL}} (Propositions 1 , 2 , and 3 ) are derived through a common two-step procedure: an anchor-wise lower bound followed by a class-wise lower bound. We state these two steps as Lemmas 3 and 4 , and then apply them sequentially to obtain each objective. SCL and BCL differ in their negative class weights, while FBCL additionally modifies the aggregation of anchor-wise losses. We unify this difference by introducing a coefficient w k w_{k} on each negative class, where w k = B k w_{k}=B_{k} for SCL and w k = 1 w_{k}=1 for BCL and FBCL.

sections.heading: B.6 Balancing components in FBCL
sections.text: As described in Section 4.2 , FBCL contains three balancing components: positive balancing (PB), which averages over positive samples as in SCL; negative balancing (NB), which averages negative samples per class in the denominator as in BCL; and structural balancing (SB), which normalizes the aggregation of anchor-wise losses. The following equation marks each method within the FBCL loss: ℒ FBCL ( Z ; Y , ℬ ) = − 1 K ∑ y ∈ [ K ] 1 B y ⏟ SB ∑ i ∈ ℬ y 1 B y − 1 ∑ j ∈ ℬ y \ { i } ⏟ PB log ( exp ⁡ ( z i ⋅ z j ) ∑ k ∈ [ K ] 1 B k ⏟ NB ​ ∑ m ∈ ℬ k exp ⁡ ( z i ⋅ z m ) ) . \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FBCL}}(Z;Y,\mathcal{B})=-\frac{1}{K}\sum_{y\in[K]}\;\underbrace{\frac{1}{B_{y}}}_{\text{SB}}\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}_{y}}\;\underbrace{\frac{1}{B_{y}-1}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{B}_{y}\backslash\{i\}}}_{\text{PB}}\;\log\Big(\frac{\exp(z_{i}\cdot z_{j})}{\sum\limits_{k\in[K]}\;\underbrace{\frac{1}{B_{k}}}_{\text{NB}}\;\sum\limits_{m\in\mathcal{B}_{k}}\exp(z_{i}\cdot z_{m})}\Big). For positive balancing, we include the summation of positive samples so that a method without balancing corresponds to SimCLR.

sections.heading: FBCL loss in practice.
sections.text: As we discussed in Section 6 , our analysis follows the standard setting where each batch contains all classes. We also note that the temperature rate is fixed to τ = 1 \tau=1 in our theory, since the value does not affect the theory. In our settings, we adopt the temperature rate used in the baseline methods for a fair comparison. But in practice, the representation space is usually affected by the value of the temperature rate under both balanced and imbalanced distributions ( Wang and Liu, 2021 ; Kukleva et al., 2023 ) . We hope that further studies investigate the attainability of a regular simplex under a large-batch training regime and its relation to temperature. Since the goal of our work is not to attain state-of-the-art results, we carefully conduct experiments to do a fair comparison with the baseline methods. We use the following loss in practice: ℒ FBCL ( Z ; Y , ℬ ) = − 1 | 𝒴 ℬ | ∑ y ∈ 𝒴 ℬ 1 B y ∑ i ∈ ℬ y 1 B y ∑ j ∈ ( ℬ y ∪ { c y } ) \ { i } log ( exp ⁡ ( z i ⋅ z j / τ ) ∑ k ∈ [ K ] 1 B k + 1 ​ ∑ m ∈ ( ℬ k ∪ { c k } ) exp ⁡ ( z i ⋅ z m / τ ) ) , \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FBCL}}(Z;Y,\mathcal{B})=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}_{\mathcal{B}}|}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}_{\mathcal{B}}}\frac{1}{B_{y}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}_{y}}\frac{1}{B_{y}}\sum_{j\in(\mathcal{B}_{y}\cup\{c_{y}\})\backslash\{i\}}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\log\Bigg(\frac{\exp(z_{i}\!\cdot\!z_{j}/\tau)}{\sum\limits_{k\in[K]}\!\frac{1}{B_{k}+1}\!\!\!\!\!\!\sum\limits_{m\in(\mathcal{B}_{k}\cup\{c_{k}\})}\!\!\!\!\!\exp(z_{i}\!\cdot\!z_{m}/\tau)}\!\Bigg), (150) where 𝒴 ℬ \mathcal{Y}_{\mathcal{B}} is the index set of class labels in the batch ℬ \mathcal{B} , and { c y } \{c_{y}\} are class-complemented pairs. The difference between practice and our theory lies in the class distribution of the anchors. Our theory assumes that the anchor classes cover the entire label set, [ K ] [K] , whereas in practice, the set of anchor classes depends on the mini-batch composition. Thus, increasing the batch size is expected to improve class coverage and make the practical objective potentially encouraging a regular simplex geometry even on large-scale datasets . In our experiments, however, the batch size was limited by GPU memory, and we leave a systematic investigation of this regime to future work. To further analyze this regime, simply increasing the batch size may still be insufficient for severe long-tailed datasets. For example, ImageNet-LT contains 1,000 classes, and even with a batch size of 1,024, few-shot classes may appear only rarely as anchors. One possible extension is therefore to augment the anchor set with class prototypes of few-shot classes. In particular, the same class prototypes introduced as complementary contrastive pairs could serve as anchors for few-shot classes, increasing their anchor coverage without requiring substantially larger mini-batches. We leave the theoretical and empirical study of such prototype-based anchor augmentation for future work.

sections.heading: ImageNet-LT and iNaturalist.
sections.text: Our setting mainly follows Zhu et al. (2022) . When combining with other methods, we follow their settings and add structural balancing. For ImageNet-LT, we train the model for 90 epochs with learning rate 0.1, and weight decay × 10 − 4 5\!\times\!10^{-4} . For iNaturalist, we train for 100 epochs with learning rate 0.2, and weight decay × 10 − 4 1\!\times\!10^{-4} . For both datasets, we use a batch size of 256, cosine scheduling for learning rate, and set λ = 1.0 \lambda=1.0 and μ = 0.35 \mu=0.35 . Class-complement ( Zhu et al., 2022 ) is used during training to incorporate class centers as additional contrastive pairs, allowing all classes to appear in every mini-batch. For SCL, class-complement is not used as Zhu et al. (2022) reported performance degradation when used. SimCLR also does not use class-complement as it is a self-supervised method. The temperature is set to τ = 0.07 \tau=0.07 . All models are trained using SGD with momentum 0.9, using four RTX 4090 GPUs.

sections.heading: CIFAR-100-LT.
sections.text: For CIFAR-100, we train the model for 200 epochs with learning rate warmed up to 0.15 within the first 5 epochs, decaying at 160 and 180 with a step size 0.1, and weight decay 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} . We set the temperature to τ = 0.1 \tau=0.1 , and set λ = 2.0 \lambda=2.0 and μ = 0.6 \mu=0.6 . All models are trained using SGD with momentum 0.9, using one RTX 4090 GPU.

sections.heading: Linear evaluation
sections.text: The linear evaluation protocol follows Chen et al. (2020) ; Oh and Lee (2024) . Specifically, we divide the training dataset into a train set and a validation set as shown in Table 5 and tune the regularization parameter by minimizing the L2-regularized cross-entropy objective using L-BFGS. Images are only resized and 224 × 224 224\times 224 center-cropped. With the best parameter, we retrain the linear classifier using both training and validation splits and then report the test accuracy.

sections.heading: Fine-tuning protocol
sections.text: We divide the training dataset into a train set and a validation set as in linear evaluation. Training images are resized and randomly cropped to 224 × 224 224\times 224 , and then randomly horizontally flipped. We perform grid search over the number of epochs, learning rate, and weight decay using the validation split with SGD with momentum 0.9 0.9 . With the best hyperparameters, we retrain using both training and validation splits and then report the model accuracy on the test set. sections.heading: C.4 Toy Experiment
sections.text: The detailed settings of the toy dataset used in Section 4.3 follow Oh and Lee (2024) . The dataset consists of five classes, each following a Gaussian distribution with orthogonal mean vectors and a shared isotropic covariance matrix with a scale of 0.15. The mean vectors are obtained from the left singular vectors of a random matrix sampled from a standard Gaussian. The data dimension is set to 6, and the class cardinalities are 500,250,100 , 50 , 25 500,250,100,50,25 . The first class is treated as the many class, the second class as the medium class, and the remaining three classes as few classes. The test dataset consists of 500 samples, with 100 samples per class. We use a two-layer MLP backbone with 32 hidden dimensions, followed by a classifier. For the cross-entropy baseline, we train the backbone and classifier for 2000 epochs. For contrastive objectives, we first train the backbone model for 2000 epochs and then train the classifier for 400 epochs. We use SGD with learning rate 0.1 0.1 , weight decay 5 ​ e − 4 5e-4 , and temperature 0.25 0.25 for contrastive training. For the intra-class variance analysis, we first compute the within-class variance and the between-class variance from the learned representations. Let S W S_{W} and S B S_{B} denote the within-class and between-class variances, respectively, and let S T = S W + S B S_{T}=S_{W}+S_{B} be the total variance. For each class y y , we compute the class-wise intra-class variance and normalize it using S T S_{T} . We then report the average normalized intra-class variance for each group. This normalization allows us to compare how much variance each class retains relative to the overall representation variance.

sections.heading: C.7 Class balanced sampling and other reweighting strategies
sections.text: One could expect structural balancing to be similar to conventional re-weighting, since both introduce class-dependent weighting, or that class-balanced sampling could provide a similar effect by constructing batches with a more uniform class distribution. However, prior studies have shown that re-balancing through class-balanced sampling or loss re-weighting (classification losses) can impair representation quality ( Kang et al., 2020 ; Zhou et al., 2020 ) . This motivates examining whether similar strategies are effective for contrastive objectives and how structural balancing differs from them. We therefore compare structural balancing with class-balanced sampling and representative re-weighting strategies. Class-balanced sampling ( CB-sampling ) constructs batches with a more uniform class distribution, but changes the original data distribution and can degrade performance ( Kang et al., 2020 ) . Re-weighting applies a weight determined by the class prior to each loss N K ​ N y \frac{N}{KN_{y}} , while class-balanced weighting ( CB-weighting ) uses the effective number of samples, 1 − β 1 − β N y \frac{1-\beta}{1-\beta^{N_{y}}} ( Cui et al., 2019 ) , with β = 0.99 \beta=0.99 . (SCL with CB-weighting corresponds to Zhong et al. (2022) ). RCL ( De Alvis et al., 2025 ) instead introduces balancing based on class priors within the logarithmic term of the contrastive loss. Note that in the full-batch setting, both are same, but such a setting is not practical for large-scale datasets, and in a mini-batch setting when re-weighting does not exactly compensate for the class imbalance, the resulting objective retains dependency on class frequency. In addition, re-weighting does not consistently improve performance as the imbalance becomes more severe . This suggests that conventional re-weighting is not always beneficial for contrastive objectives and can even degrade performance depending on class imbalance. Although structural balancing takes a similar form, it is derived from the class frequency dependence arising from the aggregation of contrastive losses. Our analysis shows that it removes this dependence in the lower bound and recovers the optimal representation geometry. Also, while re-weighting has been reported to impair representation learning when applied to classification losses, our results show that a re-weighting mechanism derived from the structure of a contrastive objective with a theoretical guarantee can instead be beneficial , motivating further re-weighting strategies specifically designed for contrastive learning.

However, although prior analyses suggest that their optimal representations may exhibit a regular simplex geometry, whether such a geometry is indeed exhibited remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we present a theoretical framework for these objectives that characterizes whether a regular simplex is formed at the optimum. By applying this to representative objectives, we show that these objectives fail to form a regular simplex at the optimum because they remain dependent on the number of samples per class. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce structural balancing that can be applied to contrastive objectives, and propose a fully balanced contrastive objective that provably forms a regular simplex geometry at its optimum. Both theoretical and empirical results demonstrate that the proposed method yields a more balanced representation space and improves performance on long-tailed recognition and transfer learning tasks. 1 Introduction Deep learning has achieved remarkable success over the past decade, yet much of this progress relies on highly curated, balanced datasets ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ; Deng et al., 2009 ) , while real-world data often exhibit long-tailed distributions, in which a small number of head classes are represented by abundant samples while a large number of tail classes contain only a few samples ( Van Horn et al., 2018 ) . Models trained under such long-tailed distributions tend to learn skewed decision boundaries, which in turn degrades generalization performance on tail classes ( Cao et al., 2019 ; Ren et al., 2020 ) . Supervised contrastive objectives have shown promising results in learning representations from long-tailed distributions ( Kang et al., 2021 ; Wang et al., 2021 ; Cui et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2022b ; Zhu et al., 2022 ; Cui et al., 2023 ; Hou et al., 2023 ; Du et al., 2024 ; De Alvis et al., 2025 ; Yi et al., 2025 ) . As in balanced distributions ( Graf et al., 2021 ; Yi et al., 2026 ) , characterizing an optimum of a loss is important for understanding the representation geometry the loss favors. However, the representation spaces induced at the minimum of these objectives remain insufficiently understood under long-tailed distributions. Among existing methods, balanced contrastive learning (BCL) ( Zhu et al., 2022 ) showed that the loss is minimized if and only if the class centers form a regular simplex, suggesting that the ideal geometry remains optimal even under long-tailed distributions. In this paper, we establish a theoretical framework for determining whether a regular simplex is a global minimizer of a supervised contrastive objective under long-tailed distributions. We first reduce the analysis from the feature space to the class-wise center space by deriving a lower bound of the loss, whose equality condition corresponds to class collapse. We then show that a center configuration that does not minimize the lower bound cannot minimize the original loss. Finally, we derive a condition that the lower bound must satisfy for a regular simplex to be its minimizer. We apply this framework to two widely used objectives for long-tailed recognition, SCL ( Khosla et al., 2020 ) and BCL, and prove that the regular simplex is not a global minimizer of either loss. Fig. 1 shows this behavior with ImageNet samples. SCL BCL FBCL (Ours) (a) 1 : 1 : 1 SCL BCL FBCL (Ours) (b) 1000 : 10 : 1 Figure 1: Visualizations of embedding spaces learned by three contrastive objectives (SCL, BCL, and FBCL) on a subset of ImageNet: three random classes sampled under (a) a balanced setting and (b) an imbalanced setting with class cardinality ratios of 1:1:1 and 1000:10:1, respectively. Angles are measured between class centers. Under (a), all three methods form a regular simplex; under (b), only FBCL forms it, whereas SCL and BCL fail. We further investigate why this result holds by examining how class imbalance affects the loss. From a balancing perspective, SCL and BCL adjust the loss only within the contrastive loss defined for each anchor, the sample for which the contrastive loss is computed. Consequently, as the losses for individual anchors are aggregated into the overall loss, the absence of balancing this aggregation leaves the loss dependent on the number of samples per class. This dependence is inherited by the lower bound, preventing the regular simplex from being a minimizer of the objective. Motivated by this observation, we present structural balancing, a method applicable to supervised contrastive objectives that balances the aggregation across anchors and removes the remaining dependence on the number of samples per class. Based on structural balancing, we propose Fully Balanced Contrastive Learning (FBCL), whose global minimizer is a regular simplex. We also analyze the effect of structural balancing on the representation space by examining how the loss penalizes the intra-class variance of each class as the loss is minimized. Under SCL and BCL, the coefficient of the intra-class variance penalty is approximately proportional to class frequency, whereas under FBCL it is approximately independent of it. This suggests more balanced contraction across classes, which is further supported by our empirical analysis of intra-class variance. We further evaluate FBCL with other contrastive objectives and apply structural balancing to other long-tailed recognition methods. Results show that FBCL and structural balancing can be effectively combined with other methods and improve their performance. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We establish a framework for determining whether a regular simplex is a global minimizer of a supervised contrastive objective under long-tailed distributions. Applying this framework to SCL and BCL, we prove that the regular simplex is a global minimizer of neither loss. • We observe that this failure occurs as a result of the remaining dependence on the number of samples per class in the loss. Based on this observation, we present structural balancing and propose Fully Balanced Contrastive Learning (FBCL), whose loss removes this dependence and admits the regular simplex as its global minimizer. • We empirically evaluate FBCL on long-tailed recognition and transfer learning, and further examine structural balancing in combination with other methods. The results show consistent improvements in classification accuracy and transferability across these settings. 2 Related Work Long-Tailed Recognition. Numerous approaches have been proposed to address long-tailed recognition. Re-sampling ( He and Garcia, 2009 ; Buda et al., 2018 ; Shi et al., 2023 ) and re-weighting classification losses ( Huang et al., 2016 ; Ren et al., 2018 ; Cui et al., 2019 ) were earlier methods in which the former balances the number of training samples and the latter assigns different weights to each training sample. Zhou et al. (2020) and Kang et al. (2020) propose a two-branch network and a two-stage learning framework, respectively, and show that such designs often yield better representations. Several works further demonstrate the effectiveness of these frameworks ( Wang et al., 2021 ; Zhong et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2022a ; Li et al., 2024a ) . Logit adjustment methods ( Cao et al., 2019 ; Menon et al., 2021 ; Kini et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2022a ; Wang et al., 2023 ) enlarge the margins for tail classes. Transfer learning methods ( Yin et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2024a ) enrich tail class features by leveraging abundant information from head classes. Recently, fine-tuning foundation models ( Tian et al., 2022 ; Dong et al., 2023 ; Shi et al., 2024 ) has proven effective with efficient training schemes, yet the impact of imbalanced data on fine-tuning is not fully understood. Contrastive Learning under Long-Tailed Distributions. Contrastive learning ( He et al., 2020 ; Chen et al., 2020 ) has shown significant progress in representation learning, mostly under balanced data distributions. To address long-tailed distributions, Hybrid-SC ( Wang et al., 2021 ) incorporates the SCL loss into the feature learning branch of a two-branch network, leveraging the quality of its learned embeddings to obtain more discriminative representations. However, subsequent studies have shown that SCL itself is biased toward head classes and yields a skewed representation space ( Kang et al., 2021 ; Cui et al., 2021 ; Zhu et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2022b ) . To mitigate this issue, PaCo ( Cui et al., 2021 ) introduces parametric class-wise learnable centers, KCL ( Kang et al., 2021 ) uses the same number of positive samples for all classes, and BCL ( Zhu et al., 2022 ) balances the negative terms so that each class contributes equally to the repulsive force. TSC ( Li et al., 2022b ) assigns uniformly distributed class targets to attract the features of each class. Yi et al. (2025) demonstrates that the geometry of the representation obtained by minimizing the SCL loss is skewed under a specific scenario where all classes share the same number of samples except for one majority class. Different from previous works, we provide a framework for analyzing whether a regular simplex is a global minimizer of supervised contrastive learning objectives under long-tailed distributions, based on the form of their lower bounds. Using our framework, we study two representative objectives: the supervised contrastive loss ( Khosla et al., 2020 ) and the balanced contrastive loss ( Zhu et al., 2022 ) , both of which continue to serve as widely used bases for analysis in long-tailed recognition ( Cui et al., 2021 ; Cui et al., 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024b ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Yi et al., 2025 ; Son et al., 2025 ; De Alvis et al., 2025 ; Wan et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . We show that the regular simplex is not a global minimizer of either objective which is nontrivial for BCL, which has been shown to admit such geometry at its minimum. Building on our framework, we propose a balancing method for supervised contrastive objectives and a fully balanced contrastive loss, a simple contrastive objective whose global minimizer is provably a regular simplex under long-tailed distributions. 3 Preliminaries We consider a K K -class classification task and learn a mapping from input data to their associated target labels.
